builtin_functions.notes: round()/abs() stay with B02 integers_floats; ord/chr with B03. sum/max/min here use several arguments, ranges and strings only, because lists are in B06 (parallel batch): B06 lists should teach len/sum/max/min of a list and encompass builtin_functions.sum_max_min. any()/all() and summing booleans need iterables of booleans, so they are left to B07 list_comprehensions (generator expressions); sorted() and key= are B06 sorting / B08 higher_order_functions; map/filter are B08; isinstance is B11; divmod/pow were left out (operators // % ** cover them).

functions.notes: Entry is builtin_functions.call_anatomy (calling before defining, as py4e does). Parameters, return values and scope are owned by their own concepts. Functions as objects (passing/storing functions, MIT L8, 100 Days 'functions in a dict') are B08 higher_order_functions; lambda is B08; recursion is B08. try/except inside helper functions (cs50p get_int) is B09.

parameters_arguments.notes: *args/**kwargs and keyword-only/positional-only markers (*, /) are B08 args_kwargs. mutable_default_trap needs lists, so it carries pending_prerequisites concept:lists and concept:mutability_aliasing; if B06 also wrote a mutable-default topic, the stitching pass should keep one. Passing a list into a function and mutating it is B06 mutability_aliasing.

return_values.notes: multiple_return_values teaches only return a, b and unpacking into names; B06 tuples/unpacking should encompass it rather than re-teach it. Breaking out of nested loops via return (B04 note) is a practice item in early_return. Pure vs side-effecting functions as a concept is B08 pure_functions, which can build on decomposition.one_job_per_function.

scope.notes: Enclosing scope, nonlocal and the full LEGB rule belong to B08 closures. Module-level scope across files is B13 modules_imports.

docstrings.notes: Doctests are left to B09 unit_testing. specifications is non-core (MIT, Code in Place only) but feeds abstraction and B09 testing/defensive_programming.

type_hints.notes: Generic container hints (list[int], dict[str, int], tuple[int, int]) belong to B06/B07 when those types are taught; checking hints with mypy is B09 tool_mypy. Reconciliation: container hints (list[int], dict[str, int], tuple[...]) were added as collection_hints; tool_mypy and lib_sqlalchemy.relationships depend on it.

decomposition.notes: Meta-skill taught as three problem-based topics (Parsons, refactoring, fill-in). Function naming conventions (deferred from B01 pep8_style) live in one_job_per_function KP3. Module-level decomposition (own modules) is B13; class-level design is B12.

abstraction.notes: Procedural abstraction only. Data abstraction and the OOP 'abstraction pillar' (bootdev, codecademy, MIT L17) belong to B11/B12.

pseudocode.notes: Only cs50p teaches it, so one non-core topic. Flowcharts (100 Days Day 7) were not given a topic.

computational_thinking.notes: One non-core topic on algorithms (declarative vs imperative, precision, tracing). Its parts decomposition and abstraction have their own topics; guess-and-check, bisection and Newton are B14.

karel_robot.notes: Non-core: needs a Karel world embedded in the platform (Code in Place / Reeborg). Placed after functions, so it serves as practice for defining commands rather than as a first-week entry point.

main_guard.notes: Needs import to show its point, so it has pending_prerequisites concept:modules_imports (B13, a later wave). The plain main() pattern without the guard is core and lives in functions.main_and_helpers, so B09 unit_testing can depend on that if it should not wait for B13.

topics.title: Calling functions: arguments in, a result out
topics.summary: Read and write calls to built-in functions as name(arguments) that produce a value, nest calls, tell functions from methods, and avoid hiding a built-in behind a variable.

knowledge_points.title: A call: name, arguments in parentheses, a result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = abs(-7)
print(n + len("hello"))   # 12
You have already called print, input, len, int, round and abs: each takes arguments and gives back a value you can store or use.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify the function name, the arguments and the result in a call; predict the value of expressions that combine calls with arithmetic.

knowledge_points.title: Nested calls run from the inside out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len(str(2 ** 10)))   # 4
2 ** 10 is 1024, str() makes "1024", len() counts 4 characters, print shows it. int(input("Age: ")) works the same way.
knowledge_points.practice: Number the order in which the calls in a nested expression run; predict the printed result.

knowledge_points.title: Functions vs methods
knowledge_points.worked_example:
word = "hi"
print(len(word))      # 2: a function, the value goes inside ()
print(word.upper())   # HI: a method, called on the value with a dot
word.len() raises AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'len'.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify calls as function or method calls; fix calls written the wrong way round (s.len(), upper(s)).

knowledge_points.title: Don't reuse a built-in's name for a variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
len = 3
print(len("hi"))
# TypeError: 'int' object is not callable
The name len now means 3. Rename the variable (length = 3).
knowledge_points.practice: Find the line that hides a built-in and explain the TypeError; pick safe variable names from a list.

topics.title: Built-ins that replace loops: sum(), max() and min()
topics.summary: Use max() and min() on several values or a string and sum() on a range instead of writing accumulator loops, and know what happens with empty input.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() of several values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(max(3, 9, 4))        # 9
print(min(2.5, -1, 0))     # -1
print(max("pear", "apple")) # pear: strings compare alphabetically
knowledge_points.practice: Predict max/min of mixed lists of arguments, including strings; rewrite an if-chain that finds the larger of two numbers as one max() call.

knowledge_points.title: sum() of a range replaces the accumulator loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(sum(range(1, 101)))     # 5050
print(sum(range(0, 11, 2)))   # 30: 0+2+4+6+8+10
Same result as total = 0 / for i in range(...): total += i, in one line.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a running-total loop as sum(range(...)); predict sums, watching the excluded stop value.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() of one string compare its characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(max("hello"))   # o
print(min("Hello"))   # H: capitals have smaller codes than lowercase letters
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the largest and smallest character of short strings, including mixed case and digits.

knowledge_points.title: Empty and single inputs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(sum(range(0)))   # 0
max("")   # ValueError: max() iterable argument is empty
max(5)    # TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable
One argument must be something to loop over; give two or more numbers to compare numbers.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each call returns a value or raises an error, and which error.

topics.title: Finding out how to call a function: help() and dir()
topics.summary: Read a function's signature and description with help(), spot optional arguments, and check which methods a type has with dir().

knowledge_points.title: help(name) shows the signature and what it does
knowledge_points.worked_example:
help(len)
# len(obj, /)
#     Return the number of items in a container.
Pass the function itself, without parentheses: help(len), not help(len()).
knowledge_points.practice: Use help() output to answer how many arguments a function takes and what it returns; fix help(len()) and help("len")-style mistakes.

knowledge_points.title: name=value in a signature marks an optional argument
knowledge_points.worked_example:
help(round)
# round(number, ndigits=None)
ndigits has a default, so round(2.567) and round(2.567, 2) both work.
knowledge_points.practice: Read signatures and decide which calls are valid; predict results of calls that omit optional arguments.

knowledge_points.title: dir() and help() for methods
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("upper" in dir(str))   # True
help(str.upper)   # shows how str.upper is called
dir(str) lists every method strings have.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether a method exists for strings; use help(str.<method>) output to choose the right method for a task.

topics.title: Defining and calling your own function
topics.summary: Write a def with an indented body, call it as many times as needed, and fix the common errors: calling before defining, missing parentheses, missing indentation.

knowledge_points.title: def creates a function; calling it runs the body
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Welcome.")

greet()
# Hello!
# Welcome.
The indented lines are the body; greet() runs them.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of short programs with one function and one call; write a function that prints a given two-line message.

knowledge_points.title: Defining does not run it; each call runs it again
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def cheer():
    print("Go!")

print("start")
cheer()
cheer()
# start
# Go!
# Go!
Nothing prints at the def; every call runs the whole body.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs when a function is defined but called zero, one or several times.

knowledge_points.title: Call after the def, and with parentheses
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cheer()   # NameError: name 'cheer' is not defined
def cheer():
    print("Go!")
Python runs top to bottom, so the def must run before the call. Writing cheer without () names the function but does not call it.
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a program prints nothing or raises NameError; reorder lines so every call comes after its def.

knowledge_points.title: The body must be indented and not empty
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet():
print("hi")
# IndentationError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1
Indent the body; use pass as a placeholder for a function you will write later.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix indentation errors in function definitions; decide which lines belong to the body.

topics.title: Tracing calls: where the program goes and comes back
topics.summary: Trace programs where functions call other functions, including calls inside loops, predicting the exact order of the output.

knowledge_points.title: A call jumps into the function and comes back
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def middle():
    print("2")

print("1")
middle()
print("3")
# 1
# 2
# 3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output order; number the lines in the order they run.

knowledge_points.title: A function can call another function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def line():
    print("-----")

def title():
    line()
    print("MENU")
    line()

title()
# -----
# MENU
# -----
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of two- and three-level call chains; write a function built from calls to given helpers.

knowledge_points.title: Order of defs does not matter, only that they exist when called
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which arrangements of defs and calls run without NameError.

knowledge_points.title: Calling a function inside a loop
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines a loop of calls prints; trace a loop that calls two different functions.

topics.title: Organising a program: main() and helper functions
topics.summary: Structure a script as a main() function that calls helper functions, with one call to main() at the bottom.

knowledge_points.title: Put the program's steps in main()
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of a main()-structured program; write main() for a program from a list of helper names.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting to call main() runs nothing
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a program prints nothing; spot a stray extra main() call that runs the program twice.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a program by following main()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def main():
    show_menu()
    greet()
    show_menu()
With the helpers above this prints the menu, Hi!, then the menu again: main() decides the order, not the order of the defs.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace programs where main() calls helpers in a different order from their definitions, or calls one twice.

topics.title: Giving a function input: one parameter
topics.summary: Define a function with a parameter, call it with different arguments (literals, variables, expressions), and read TypeErrors about argument counts.

knowledge_points.title: A parameter receives the argument
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Ada")   # Hello, Ada!
greet("Bo")    # Hello, Bo!
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs for calls with different arguments; write a one-parameter function that prints a formatted message.

knowledge_points.title: Arguments can be variables or expressions; names need not match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def show_square(n):
    print(n * n)

x = 4
show_square(x)       # 16
show_square(x + 1)   # 25
The argument is evaluated first, then its value is given to n.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs when the argument is a variable with a different name or an expression; trace the value of the parameter in each call.

knowledge_points.title: Parameter vs argument
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(n):   # n is the parameter: a name in the def
    print(n * 2)

double(7)        # 7 is the argument: the value in the call
knowledge_points.practice: Label parameters and arguments in code; choose the correct term in sentences about a program.

knowledge_points.title: Wrong number of arguments is a TypeError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
greet()
# TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'
greet("Ada", "Bo")
# TypeError: greet() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise TypeError; fix the call or the def so they match.

topics.title: Several parameters, matched by position
topics.summary: Define and call functions with two or three parameters, matching arguments by position and noticing when swapped arguments give wrong results silently.

knowledge_points.title: Arguments fill parameters left to right
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs of calls to two- and three-parameter functions; write a function with two parameters.

knowledge_points.title: Swapped arguments run but give the wrong answer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def power(base, exp):
    print(base ** exp)

power(2, 3)   # 8
power(3, 2)   # 9: no error, just a different result
describe(36, "Ada") prints 36 is Ada.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the call whose arguments are in the wrong order; predict outputs when order changes.

knowledge_points.title: Using parameters inside loops and conditions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def row(char, width):
    print(char * width)

for h in range(1, 4):
    row("#", h)
# #
# ##
# ###
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of a loop that calls a two-parameter function; write a function whose parameters control a loop.

topics.title: Keyword arguments: naming the parameter in the call
topics.summary: Call functions with name=value arguments, mix positional and keyword arguments in the allowed order, and read the errors when names clash or are misspelled.

knowledge_points.title: Name the parameter, and order no longer matters
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs of keyword calls; rewrite a positional call using keywords.

knowledge_points.title: Positional arguments first, then keyword ones
knowledge_points.worked_example:
describe("Ada", age=36)    # fine
describe(name="Ada", 36)
# SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which mixed calls are valid; fix calls that put a positional argument after a keyword one.

knowledge_points.title: A keyword must match a parameter, once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
describe("Ada", name="Bo")
# TypeError: describe() got multiple values for argument 'name'
describe(nam="Ada", age=3)
# TypeError: describe() got an unexpected keyword argument 'nam'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which error each call raises; fix misspelled or duplicated keywords.

topics.title: Default parameter values
topics.summary: Give parameters default values, override some of them positionally or by keyword, and know that defaults go last and are evaluated once.

knowledge_points.title: A default makes an argument optional
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(f"{greeting}, {name}!")

greet("Ada")          # Hello, Ada!
greet("Ada", "Hi")    # Hi, Ada!
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs with and without the optional argument; add a default to an existing function.

knowledge_points.title: Skip one default and set a later one by keyword
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def order(item, size="M", qty=1):
    print(item, size, qty)

order("tea", qty=2)   # tea M 2
order("tea", 2) would set size to 2, not qty.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the call that changes only one of several defaults; find calls that fill the wrong parameter.

knowledge_points.title: Parameters with defaults come last
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which def lines are valid; reorder parameters to fix the SyntaxError.

knowledge_points.title: The default is computed once, when def runs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
RATE = 0.1
def tax(price, rate=RATE):
    print(price * rate)

RATE = 0.2
tax(100)   # 10.0: the default was fixed at def time
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs when a variable used as a default changes after the def.

topics.title: The mutable default argument trap
topics.summary: Recognise that a list default is shared between calls, and fix it with a None default.

knowledge_points.title: A list default is shared between calls
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add("a"))   # ['a']
print(add("b"))   # ['a', 'b']: the same list as last time
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of repeated calls to a function with a list default.

knowledge_points.title: Fix: default to None and make a new list inside
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite functions with list or dict defaults using the None pattern.

knowledge_points.title: Which defaults are safe
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def f(n=0, name="", items=None):   # safe: numbers, strings and None cannot be changed in place
def g(items=[]):                   # trap: a list can
knowledge_points.practice: Classify def lines as safe or trap.

topics.title: Returning a value
topics.summary: Write functions that return a result, and use that result in assignments, expressions and as the argument of another call.

knowledge_points.title: return sends a value back to the caller
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(21)
print(result)   # 42
knowledge_points.practice: Predict stored results; write one-line functions that return a computed value.

knowledge_points.title: A call can go anywhere a value can
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values of expressions and conditions that contain calls.

knowledge_points.title: One function's result as another's argument
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def square(n):
    return n * n

print(double(square(3)))   # 18: square runs first, then double
print(square(double(3)))   # 36
knowledge_points.practice: Trace nested calls of your own functions; write a composition that computes a described result.

knowledge_points.title: A result you don't store or use is lost
knowledge_points.worked_example:
double(5)          # runs, but the 10 is thrown away
x = double(5)      # keep it
print(x)           # 10
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a program prints nothing or uses a stale value after calling a returning function.

topics.title: Printing is not returning: functions that give back None
topics.summary: Predict when a function returns None, explain why print(f()) can print None, and fix code that uses the result of a function that only prints.

knowledge_points.title: No return statement means the result is None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet():
    print("hi")

x = greet()   # prints hi
print(x)      # None
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the stored value after calling functions with and without return.

knowledge_points.title: print(f()) shows the output and then None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(greet())
# hi
# None
The function prints hi; then print shows the value greet returned: None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs of print wrapped around printing functions and returning functions.

knowledge_points.title: Using a printing function's result fails later
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

total = add(2, 3) + 1
# prints 5, then TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'
Fix: return a + b instead of printing it.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix functions that print where the caller needs a returned value.

knowledge_points.title: Choosing return or print
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h       # the caller can print it, add it, compare it
print(area(2, 3) + area(1, 4))   # 10
Return values that other code needs; print only when showing the user is the whole job.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose return or print for described functions; convert printing functions to returning ones.

topics.title: return ends the function: early exits and several returns
topics.summary: Use return inside if branches and loops to finish a function early, write guard clauses, and avoid returning too soon inside a loop.

knowledge_points.title: return stops the function at once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def f():
    print("a")
    return 1
    print("b")   # never runs

print(f())   # a, then 1
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs when statements follow a return; find unreachable lines.

knowledge_points.title: One return per branch
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results for boundary inputs; write a classifier function with several returns.

knowledge_points.title: Guard clause: deal with the bad case first
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a nested if/else as a guard clause plus a main return; predict results for the guarded case.

knowledge_points.title: return in a loop: stop at the first match, decide 'none found' after the loop
knowledge_points.practice: Fix search functions that return too early inside the loop; predict results for inputs with and without a match.

topics.title: Functions that answer yes or no
topics.summary: Write predicate functions such as is_even that return True or False directly, and use them in if and while conditions.

knowledge_points.title: A predicate returns True or False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict predicate results; write predicates such as is_positive or is_vowel.

knowledge_points.title: Return the condition itself, not if/else True/False
knowledge_points.practice: Shorten verbose predicates to one return; combine conditions with and/or inside the return.

knowledge_points.title: Use predicates in if and while
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs of loops and branches that call predicates; fill in the condition using a predicate and not.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: testing the function instead of calling it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
if is_even:          # always true: is_even without () is the function itself
    print("even")
Write if is_even(n): instead. Also avoid if is_even(n) == True: the == True adds nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Find predicates used without parentheses or without an argument; simplify comparisons with True.

topics.title: Returning two or more values
topics.summary: Return several values with return a, b and unpack them into separate variables, matching the number of names to the number of values.

knowledge_points.title: return a, b sends back two values; unpack them with two names
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def divide(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b

q, r = divide(17, 5)
print(q, r)   # 3 2
knowledge_points.practice: Predict unpacked values; write a function that returns two computed results.

knowledge_points.title: Without unpacking you get one value holding both
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(divide(17, 5))   # (3, 2)
The parentheses show a single grouped value (a tuple; more on these with lists and tuples).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether a call prints a pair or two separate values.

knowledge_points.title: The number of names must match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
q, r, x = divide(17, 5)
# ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 2)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which unpacking lines raise ValueError; fix them.

topics.title: Local variables: each call has its own
topics.summary: Predict which variables exist where: names created inside a function, including parameters, are local to each call and invisible outside it.

knowledge_points.title: Variables made inside a function exist only during the call
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_total():
    total = 5
    return total

make_total()
print(total)
# NameError: name 'total' is not defined
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which prints succeed and which raise NameError; fix by using the returned value.

knowledge_points.title: Changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_one(n):
    n = n + 1
    return n

x = 5
add_one(x)
print(x)            # 5
x = add_one(x)      # 6: store the result to change x
knowledge_points.practice: Trace caller and function variables side by side; predict values after calls.

knowledge_points.title: Same name in two functions, two different variables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def a():
    count = 1
    return count

def b():
    count = 2
    return count

print(a(), b())   # 1 2
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs where several functions reuse a local name.

knowledge_points.title: No separate scope for if and for blocks inside a function
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether names set inside loops or ifs are visible later in the same function; spot the NameError when the loop never runs.

topics.title: Global variables and the global statement
topics.summary: Read global constants inside functions, predict what assignment inside a function does to a global, fix UnboundLocalError, and prefer returning values over global.

knowledge_points.title: Functions can read global variables
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of functions that read globals, including after the global changes before the call.

knowledge_points.title: Assigning inside a function makes a new local
knowledge_points.worked_example:
score = 0

def reset():
    score = 10   # a new local score

reset()
print(score)   # 0: the global is unchanged
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the global's value after calls that assign to the same name.

knowledge_points.title: Reading then assigning: UnboundLocalError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count = 0

def inc():
    count += 1

inc()
# UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value
The assignment makes count local, so it has no value yet when += reads it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which functions raise UnboundLocalError.

knowledge_points.title: global lets a function rebind; returning is usually better
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def inc():
    global count
    count += 1
# better: pass and return
def inc(n):
    return n + 1
count = inc(count)
knowledge_points.practice: Fix an UnboundLocalError both ways; rewrite a global-modifying function to take a parameter and return.

topics.title: Documenting a function with a docstring
topics.summary: Write a one-line or multi-line docstring as the first statement of a function and read it back with help().

knowledge_points.title: A string as the first line of the body
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(w, h):
    """Return the area of a w-by-h rectangle."""
    return w * h
A docstring says what the function does and returns; a # comment explains a line of code.
knowledge_points.practice: Add one-line docstrings to given functions; choose the best docstring for a function from options.

knowledge_points.title: help() shows your docstring
knowledge_points.worked_example:
help(area)
# area(w, h)
#     Return the area of a w-by-h rectangle.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what help() shows for functions with and without docstrings.

knowledge_points.title: Only the first statement counts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def f():
    x = 1
    """Not a docstring."""
    return x
help(f) shows no description: the string is not the first statement.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which strings are docstrings; move misplaced ones.

knowledge_points.title: Multi-line docstrings: summary, blank line, details
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def bmi(kg, m):
    """Return body-mass index.

    kg: weight in kilograms
    m: height in metres
    """
    return kg / m ** 2
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of a multi-line docstring; write one that names each parameter and the result.

topics.title: Specifications: what a function promises
topics.summary: Write and read function specifications with preconditions (what the caller must provide) and postconditions (what the function guarantees), and test code against them.

knowledge_points.title: A spec states inputs and result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def sum_to(n):
    """Return 1 + 2 + ... + n.

    Requires: n is an int, n >= 1.
    """
The Requires line is the precondition; the Return line is the postcondition.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify the precondition and postcondition in docstrings; predict results from the spec alone.

knowledge_points.title: Breaking the precondition is the caller's fault
knowledge_points.worked_example: sum_to(-3) may return anything: the spec only promises results for n >= 1. The function is not buggy; the call is.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide for given calls whether the caller or the function is at fault when results look wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Test an implementation against its spec
knowledge_points.practice: Find a valid input where an implementation breaks its spec; fix it.

knowledge_points.title: Write a spec for an existing function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def average(total, count):
    return total / count
# Spec: Return the mean. Requires: count > 0.
The precondition records the case that would crash (count = 0 raises ZeroDivisionError).
knowledge_points.practice: Choose or write the precondition that rules out crashing inputs; pick the spec that matches the code.

topics.title: Type hints on parameters and return values
topics.summary: Annotate a function's parameters and return type, read annotated signatures, and know that Python does not enforce hints at run time.

knowledge_points.title: Annotate parameters and the return type
knowledge_points.practice: Add hints to given functions; read a signature and say what types go in and come out.

knowledge_points.title: -> None for functions that only print
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right return hint for printing and returning functions.

knowledge_points.title: Hints are not checked when the code runs
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs of calls that ignore the hints; spot calls that disagree with the hints.

knowledge_points.title: Annotating variables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
count: int = 0
name: str = "Ada"
print(count, name)   # 0 Ada
The hint documents the intended type; assignment works as usual.
knowledge_points.practice: Annotate variables; find the annotation that disagrees with its value.

topics.title: Hints with | : values that may be None or one of several types
topics.summary: Write hints such as int | None and int | float, and use them to spot code that forgets the None case.

knowledge_points.title: X | None for a function that may return None
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the return hint for functions that sometimes return None.

knowledge_points.title: int | float, and int is accepted where float is expected
knowledge_points.practice: Pick hints that accept every intended argument type.

knowledge_points.title: Hints reveal the forgotten None case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
d = safe_divide(1, 0)   # None
print(d + 1)   # TypeError
The hint int | None warns the caller to check: if d is not None: ...
knowledge_points.practice: Fix callers that use an Optional result without checking for None.

topics.title: Type hints for collections: list[int], dict[str, float], tuple[str, str]
topics.summary: Annotate parameters, return values and variables that hold lists, dicts and tuples with their item types, and know that hints are not checked when the program runs.

knowledge_points.title: list[str]: a list and the type of its items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def first_word(words: list[str]) -> str:
    return words[0]

print(first_word(["hi", "there"]))  # hi
The type in square brackets says what every item is; a plain list hint would say nothing about the items.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the right hint for described parameters (list of names, list of prices); fill in hints for short functions.

knowledge_points.title: dict[key, value]
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def price_of(prices: dict[str, float], item: str) -> float:
    return prices[item]

print(price_of({"tea": 2.5, "cake": 4.0}, "tea"))  # 2.5
A dict hint names the key type first, then the value type; set[str] works the same way with one type.
knowledge_points.practice: Write hints for dicts described in words (word counts, phone books); spot hints with key and value swapped.

knowledge_points.title: tuple[str, str] and lists of tuples
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def split_name(full: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    first, last = full.split()
    return first, last

people: list[tuple[str, int]] = [("ana", 31), ("bo", 25)]
print(split_name("Ada Lovelace"), people[1][0])  # ('Ada', 'Lovelace') bo
A tuple hint lists the type of each position; hints nest, and a variable can carry one too.
knowledge_points.practice: Match functions that return several values to their tuple hints; write the hint for a list of (name, score) records.

knowledge_points.title: Hints are not checked at run time; list(int) is a bug
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(first_word([10, 20]))  # 10: runs anyway

def total(nums: list(int)) -> int:
    return 0
# TypeError: 'type' object is not iterable
Python ignores the hint when running (first_word from KP1); a checker such as mypy reports the mismatch. Hints use square brackets, never a call.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether code with wrong-type arguments runs; fix hints written with parentheses.

topics.notes: Added in reconciliation (gap: B05 handed generic container hints to B06/B07, neither wrote them). Non-core like type_hints.optional_and_union. Snippets run with Python 3.13.

topics.title: Turning repeated code into a function
topics.summary: Spot blocks of code that repeat with small differences and replace them with one function whose parameters are the parts that differ.

knowledge_points.title: Repeated lines become one function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("*" * 10)
print("Score")
print("*" * 10)
print("*" * 10)
print("Lives")
print("*" * 10)
# becomes
def banner(text):
    print("*" * 10)
    print(text)
    print("*" * 10)
banner("Score")
banner("Lives")
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the lines that form the repeated block; reorder lines into the extracted function (Parsons).

knowledge_points.title: Whatever differs becomes a parameter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Two blocks that differ in the text and the character:
def banner(text, char):
    print(char * 10)
    print(text)
    print(char * 10)
knowledge_points.practice: Given two or three similar blocks, decide which values become parameters and write the call for each block.

knowledge_points.title: A repeated calculation becomes a returning function
knowledge_points.practice: Replace a formula written out several times with a function and calls.

knowledge_points.title: Fix once, fixed everywhere
knowledge_points.worked_example: If the formula above had 5 / 8 by mistake in three copied places, all three need fixing; in to_celsius, one edit fixes every call.
knowledge_points.practice: Count how many edits a change needs before and after extracting a function; fix a bug in a shared helper.

topics.title: Top-down design: outline main(), then fill in helpers
topics.summary: Break a task into named steps written as calls in main(), run the outline with stub helpers, and refine each helper in turn.

knowledge_points.title: Write main() as a list of named steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def main():
    price = ask_price()
    tip = compute_tip(price)
    show_total(price, tip)
Each line names one step; the details come later.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder helper calls into a working main() for a described program (Parsons); name the steps of a task.

knowledge_points.title: Stubs let the outline run before it is finished
knowledge_points.practice: Write stubs for given helper names so main() runs; predict output of a stubbed program.

knowledge_points.title: Refine a step that is still too big
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def play_round():
    show_board()
    move = ask_move()
    apply_move(move)
A helper can itself be split into helpers, level by level.
knowledge_points.practice: Split a long described step into two to four helper calls.

knowledge_points.title: Fill in a helper and test it on its own
knowledge_points.practice: Implement one helper of a given outline so that its test calls print the expected values.

topics.title: One job per function: separating input, work and output
topics.summary: Split code that mixes input, calculation and printing into functions that each do one job, with descriptive verb names in snake_case.

knowledge_points.title: Separate getting input, computing and showing
knowledge_points.practice: Sort the lines of a mixed program into input, computing and output functions (Parsons).

knowledge_points.title: Computing functions return; they do not print or ask
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite computing functions that print or call input() so they take parameters and return.

knowledge_points.title: Name functions for what they do
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def calc(x): ...        # vague
def to_celsius(f): ...  # verb phrase, snake_case
def is_valid(code): ... # is_/has_ for True/False answers
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the best name for described functions; rename badly named ones.

knowledge_points.title: If the name needs 'and', split the function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def read_and_check_and_print(): ...
# becomes read_code(), is_valid(code), show_result(ok)
knowledge_points.practice: Split a function that does several jobs into named helpers and a short caller.

topics.title: Abstraction: using and generalising functions as black boxes
topics.summary: Use a function from its name and specification alone, swap implementations without changing callers, and generalise a function by turning fixed values into parameters.

knowledge_points.title: Use a function from its spec alone
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def is_leap(year):
    """Return True if year is a leap year."""
    ...
print(is_leap(2024))   # True: you need the spec, not the body
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of calls from docstrings alone (bodies hidden).

knowledge_points.title: Different insides, same behaviour
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which replacement implementations keep every caller working; find one that breaks the spec for some input.

knowledge_points.title: Generalise: turn a fixed value into a parameter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def line():
    print("-" * 10)
# generalised, old calls still work:
def line(width=10, char="-"):
    print(char * width)
line()          # ----------
line(3, "=")    # ===
knowledge_points.practice: Generalise hard-coded functions with parameters and defaults so existing calls keep working.

knowledge_points.title: Code that reads at one level of detail
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def main():
    order = take_order()
    bill = price(order)
    print_receipt(bill)
main() hides how each step works; the details live one level down.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which version of a program hides detail at the right level; replace inline detail with a named call.

topics.title: Planning with pseudocode before writing code
topics.summary: Write a program's steps as plain-English comments, put them in order, translate each into Python, and spot missing steps.

knowledge_points.title: Write the steps first, as comments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# ask for the bill
# ask for the tip percent
# compute the tip
# print the total
Each comment becomes one or two lines of code underneath it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write pseudocode steps for a described small program; choose the clearest pseudocode from options.

knowledge_points.title: Put the steps in a working order
knowledge_points.worked_example: Computing the tip before asking for the percent cannot work: every step may only use what earlier steps produced.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder shuffled pseudocode lines (Parsons); find the step used before it is available.

knowledge_points.title: Translate each step into Python
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# ask for the bill
bill = float(input("Bill: "))
# if the bill is over 100, give 10% off
if bill > 100:
    bill = bill * 0.9
knowledge_points.practice: Match pseudocode lines to code; fill in the code under each comment.

knowledge_points.title: Find the step the plan forgot
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# ask for the age
# print whether the person can vote
age = input("Age: ")
if age >= 18: ...   # TypeError: the plan missed "convert to a number"
knowledge_points.practice: Find the missing pseudocode step that causes a bug, and add it.

topics.title: From a problem to precise steps: algorithms
topics.summary: Tell 'what' knowledge from 'how' knowledge, recognise instructions that are too vague or never stop, trace an algorithm by hand and turn it into a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Declarative vs imperative knowledge
knowledge_points.worked_example:
What: the GCD of a and b is the largest number dividing both.
How: while b is not 0, replace (a, b) with (b, a % b); then a is the GCD.
Only the "how" can be turned into a program.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify statements as declarative (what) or imperative (how).

knowledge_points.title: Steps must be exact and must finish
knowledge_points.worked_example:
"Make the number smaller until it is small" is vague.
"Halve n until n < 1" is exact, and stops because n keeps shrinking.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the instruction a computer could follow; decide whether a described loop always stops.

knowledge_points.title: Trace an algorithm by hand
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table for the GCD algorithm on new inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Turn the traced steps into code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a, b = 48, 18
while b != 0:
    a, b = b, a % b
print(a)   # 6
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of the algorithm (Parsons); write the loop for a described step-by-step method.

topics.title: Karel the robot: commands and new commands
topics.summary: Predict where Karel ends up after a sequence of move(), turn_left(), put_beeper() and pick_beeper(), and define new commands such as turn_right() from existing ones.

knowledge_points.title: Karel's world and four commands
knowledge_points.worked_example:
move()          # one corner forward
turn_left()     # quarter turn left
put_beeper()
pick_beeper()
Starting at (1, 1) facing east, move(); move() ends at (3, 1).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict Karel's final corner and direction after short command sequences.

knowledge_points.title: Define turn_right() from three left turns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def turn_right():
    turn_left()
    turn_left()
    turn_left()
knowledge_points.practice: Write turn_around(); predict direction after calls to the new commands.

knowledge_points.title: Build bigger commands from smaller ones
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def climb_step():
    turn_left()
    move()
    turn_right()
    move()
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder lines into a new command that solves a pictured task (Parsons); trace calls through two levels of commands.

knowledge_points.title: Errors: moving into a wall, picking from an empty corner
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Karel facing a wall: move() stops the program with an error.
pick_beeper() with no beeper on the corner also stops it.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the command in a sequence that crashes Karel in a pictured world.

topics.title: Karel with loops and conditions
topics.summary: Make Karel programs work in any world size with for, while front_is_clear() and if beepers_present(), including the last-corner fencepost case.

knowledge_points.title: Repeat a fixed number of times with for
knowledge_points.practice: Predict beepers placed and final corner; write a for loop for a fixed-length task.

knowledge_points.title: while front_is_clear(): works in any world
knowledge_points.practice: Choose between for and while for pictured worlds of unknown size; write a move-to-wall command.

knowledge_points.title: Fencepost: the last corner needs one more step
knowledge_points.worked_example:
while front_is_clear():
    put_beeper()
    move()
put_beeper()   # the corner at the wall
Without the last line the final corner is left empty.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that miss the last corner; predict beeper counts for a given width.

knowledge_points.title: Check before acting with if
knowledge_points.practice: Add the condition that prevents a crash; predict which corners end with beepers.

topics.title: Running main() only when the file is run: if __name__ == "__main__"
topics.summary: Call main() through the __name__ guard and predict which code runs when a file is run directly and when it is imported.

knowledge_points.title: __name__ is "__main__" in the file you run
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(__name__)   # __main__
Python sets __name__ for every file; it is "__main__" only for the file being run.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the value printed by print(__name__) in a run file.

knowledge_points.title: Call main() through the guard
knowledge_points.practice: Write the guard at the bottom of a main()-structured program.

knowledge_points.title: When imported, the guard keeps main() from running
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# shapes.py has def area(...) and the guard
# app.py:
import shapes
print(shapes.area(2, 3))   # 6, and shapes.main() did not run
Inside shapes.py during the import, __name__ is "shapes".
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of running one file that imports another, with and without the guard.

knowledge_points.title: Common mistakes in the guard
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix broken guards.
